claim: Telomere content was quantified across 329 cell lines profiled with WGS in the CCLE.
source: We quantified telomere content across cell lines using WGS and WES data from the independent CCLE (Barretina et al., 2012; Ghandi et al., 2019) and GDSC (Yang et al., 2013) datasets. In particular, we considered 329 cell lines profiled with WGS and 326 with WES in the CCLE, and 1056 samples profiled with WES in the GDSC, of which 55 were non-cancerous matched-normal samples.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cell lines profiled with WGS in the CCLE dataset.

evidence: The manuscript reports outlier associations between CST complex protein knockouts and telomere content.

evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that TERC contains an H/ACA box snoRNA domain.

claim: TERC is a scaRNA family member.
source: The co-expression of TERC and these other RNAs may be a consequence of their shared localization, processing, and regulation in Cajal bodies (Gall, 2003; Venteicher et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2004), as TERC itself contains an H/ACA box small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) domain (Mitchell et al., 1999) and is a scaRNA family member.
evidence: The manuscript states that TERC is a scaRNA family member.

claim: Variations in Cajal body processing may act as factors in TERC reactivation.
source: Moreover, these associations suggest that variations in Cajal body processing may act as factors in TERC reactivation (Cao et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript speculates that variations in Cajal body processing may affect TERC reactivation, citing literature.

claim: TERT enzymatic activity remains strongly correlated with raw levels of TERT expression.
source: Although we focused on the transcriptional features of telomerase, it is important to note that other factors in addition to TERT and TERC expression determine telomerase activity and the eventual maintenance of telomere length (Listerman et al., 2013). Despite these orthogonal factors, TERT enzymatic activity remains strongly correlated with raw levels of TERT expression (Takakura et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the correlation between TERT enzymatic activity and TERT expression.

claim: Other factors in addition to TERT and TERC expression determine telomerase activity and the eventual maintenance of telomere length.
source: Although we focused on the transcriptional features of telomerase, it is important to note that other factors in addition to TERT and TERC expression determine telomerase activity and the eventual maintenance of telomere length (Listerman et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that other factors determine telomerase activity.

claim: TERT promoter status was assessed for 503 cell lines across 21 cancer types using WGS and targeted sequencing.
source: First, using WGS and targeted sequencing of the TERT promoter provided in the CCLE, we assessed TERT promoter status for 503 cell lines across 21 cancer types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cell lines assessed for TERT promoter status.

claim: Only the C228T (chr5:1,295,228 C>T) mutation was significantly (p = 2.8×10−5, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test) associated with an increase in TERT expression.
source: We found that only the C228T (chr5:1,295,228 C>T) mutation was significantly (p = 2.8×10−5, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test) associated with an increase in TERT expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results showing a significant association between the C228T mutation and increased TERT expression.

claim: The mean level of TERT expression in monoallelic contexts was only slightly lower than that of biallelic contexts, with less than a 1.5-fold difference between the groups (p = 0.03, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test).
source: Surprisingly, the mean level of TERT expression in monoallelic contexts was only slightly lower than that of biallelic contexts, with less than a 1.5-fold difference between the groups (p = 0.03, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results showing a small difference in TERT expression between monoallelic and biallelic contexts.

claim: The reduced difference in TERT expression between monoallelic and biallelic contexts may be a consequence of the effects of the TERT promoter mutation in producing particularly robust monoallelic expression.
source: Given that cells with biallelic TERT expression presumably express TERT with twice the transcriptional source sites as those with monoallelic TERT expression, this reduced difference may be a consequence of the effects of the TERT promoter mutation in producing particularly robust monoallelic expression (Huang et al., 2013) or expression of TERT from multiple sites all of the same allele (Rowland et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript speculates that the reduced difference may be due to robust monoallelic expression from promoter mutations, citing literature.

claim: The reduced difference in TERT expression between monoallelic and biallelic contexts may be a consequence of expression of TERT from multiple sites all of the same allele.
source: Given that cells with biallelic TERT expression presumably express TERT with twice the transcriptional source sites as those with monoallelic TERT expression, this reduced difference may be a consequence of the effects of the TERT promoter mutation in producing particularly robust monoallelic expression (Huang et al., 2013) or expression of TERT from multiple sites all of the same allele (Rowland et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript speculates that the reduced difference may be due to expression from multiple sites on the same allele, citing literature.

claim: TERT allele-specific expression status was determined for 157 cell lines.
source: To further explore allele-specific expression (ASE) patterns of TERT, we employed an ASE-calling pipeline (Supplementary Methods) and determined TERT allele-specific expression status for 157 cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), an increase of 69 cell lines compared to a previous report using CCLE WGS data (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cell lines with determined TERT allele-specific expression status.

claim: 87 out of 157 cell lines (58.6%) express TERT from a single allele.
source: Out of these 157 cell lines, 87 (58.6%) express TERT from a single allele.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and percentage of cell lines expressing TERT from a single allele.

claim: Promoter mutations unanimously drive monoallelic expression.
source: Moreover, of these 157 cell lines, 129 have a sequenced promoter, with which we confirm that promoter mutations unanimously drive monoallelic expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The manuscript confirms that promoter mutations drive monoallelic expression in all cases examined.

claim: Several new tissues of origin in which TERT is monoallelically expressed without a mutant promoter were revealed, such as hematopoietic cell lines.
source: Our expanded set of cell lines also reveals several new tissues of origin in which TERT is monoallelically expressed without a mutant promoter, such as hematopoietic cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of new tissues with monoallelic TERT expression without promoter mutations.

claim: Promoter-wildtype monoallelic TERT expression occurred in 36% (47 of 129) of samples.
source: Compared to promoter-wildtype monoallelic TERT expression occurring in 36% (47 of 129) of samples, only 9.4% (11 out of 117) of samples expressed CLPTM1L from a single allele and 22% (5 of 22) expressed SLC6A19 from a single allele, and we were unable to assess co-occurrence due to lack of overlap in samples with heterozygous SNPs in both TERT and CLPTM1L or SLC6A19.
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of promoter-wildtype monoallelic TERT expression.

claim: 9.4% (11 out of 117) of samples expressed CLPTM1L from a single allele.
source: Compared to promoter-wildtype monoallelic TERT expression occurring in 36% (47 of 129) of samples, only 9.4% (11 out of 117) of samples expressed CLPTM1L from a single allele and 22% (5 of 22) expressed SLC6A19 from a single allele, and we were unable to assess co-occurrence due to lack of overlap in samples with heterozygous SNPs in both TERT and CLPTM1L or SLC6A19.
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of monoallelic CLPTM1L expression.

claim: 22% (5 of 22) of samples expressed SLC6A19 from a single allele.
source: Compared to promoter-wildtype monoallelic TERT expression occurring in 36% (47 of 129) of samples, only 9.4% (11 out of 117) of samples expressed CLPTM1L from a single allele and 22% (5 of 22) expressed SLC6A19 from a single allele, and we were unable to assess co-occurrence due to lack of overlap in samples with heterozygous SNPs in both TERT and CLPTM1L or SLC6A19.
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of monoallelic SLC6A19 expression.

claim: Examination of methylation patterns at the TERT locus revealed five prominent ASM clusters corresponding roughly to the upstream 5 kb region (containing the promoter), part of a CpG island overlapping the first exon, two other parts of this CpG island, and the remaining gene body.
source: Examination of methylation patterns at the TERT locus revealed five prominent ASM clusters in the TERT locus, corresponding roughly to the upstream 5 kb region (containing the promoter), part of a CpG island overlapping the first exon, two other parts of this CpG island, and the remaining gene body (Figure 3a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the identification of five ASM clusters at the TERT locus and references a figure.

claim: TERTp mutants exhibited strong and significant (p < 0.01) increases in ASM in the promoter (n = 485), remaining gene body (n = 493), and exon 1 (n = 478) regions.
source: Comparison of each region's mean ASM against TERTp mutant status revealed that TERTp mutants exhibited strong and significant (p < 0.01) increases in ASM in the promoter (n = 485), remaining gene body (n = 493), and exon 1 (n = 478) regions (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results showing increased ASM in TERTp mutants.

claim: TERTp wild-type cell lines tended to lack ASM throughout the TERT locus, instead being hypermethylated in all regions except for exon 1.
source: In contrast, TERTp wild-type cell lines tended to lack ASM throughout the TERT locus, instead being hypermethylated in all regions except for exon 1 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), and partial hypomethylation in promoter mutants may reflect the hemizygous methylation previously observed at the TERT locus (Rowland et al., 2020; Stern et al., 2015; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methylation pattern in TERTp wild-type cell lines.

claim: Partial hypomethylation in promoter mutants may reflect the hemizygous methylation previously observed at the TERT locus.
source: In contrast, TERTp wild-type cell lines tended to lack ASM throughout the TERT locus, instead being hypermethylated in all regions except for exon 1 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), and partial hypomethylation in promoter mutants may reflect the hemizygous methylation previously observed at the TERT locus (Rowland et al., 2020; Stern et al., 2015; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript speculates that partial hypomethylation may reflect hemizygous methylation, citing literature.

claim: Absolute methylation of the remaining gene body was positively correlated with TERT expression in both promoter status contexts.
source: Absolute methylation of the remaining gene body was positively correlated with TERT expression in both promoter status contexts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e), which parallels previous reports of a positive correlation between TERT expression and methylation (Barthel et al., 2017; Salgado et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports positive correlations between gene body methylation and TERT expression, citing literature.

claim: Exon 1 methylation was elevated in nearly all cell lines with monoallelic TERT expression in both the mutant promoter context (p = 6.3×10−3, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, n = 81) and the wildtype promoter context (p = 1.6×10−4, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, n = 98) compared to biallelic TERT expressors.
source: Exon 1 methylation was elevated in nearly all cell lines with monoallelic TERT expression in both the mutant promoter context (p = 6.3×10−3, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, n = 81) and the wildtype promoter context (p = 1.6×10−4, two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, n = 98) compared to biallelic TERT expressors (Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results showing elevated exon 1 methylation in monoallelic TERT expressors, citing literature.

claim: Only promoter-mutant cell lines were hypomethylated in the regions surrounding exon 1, suggesting that the epigenetic state of promoter mutants is distinct from that of promoter-wildtype monoallelic TERT expressors.
source: Interestingly, although most cell lines with monoallelic TERT expression displayed partially elevated methylation levels in exon 1 (Figure 3b), only promoter-mutant cell lines were hypomethylated in the surrounding regions, suggesting that the epigenetic state of promoter mutants is in fact distinct from that of promoter-wildtype monoallelic TERT expressors.
evidence: The manuscript infers that the epigenetic state of promoter mutants is distinct based on hypomethylation patterns.

claim: A broad genome-wide distribution of CGIs that were hypomethylated in TERTpmut samples relative to TERTpWT samples was found.
source: Surprisingly, we instead found a broad genome-wide distribution of CGIs that were hypomethylated in TERTpmut samples relative to TERTpWT samples (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of a genome-wide distribution of hypomethylated CGIs in TERTpmut samples.

claim: TERTp mutants exhibited increased levels of H3K9ac1K14ac0 and H3K9ac1K14ac1 marks.
source: Moreover, when correlated with a panel of global histone modification levels, we found that TERTp mutants exhibited increased levels of H3K9ac1K14ac0 and H3K9ac1K14ac1 marks (Figure 4b), which have been suggested as marks of transcriptionally active chromatin (Ruthenburg et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript reports increased levels of specific histone marks in TERTp mutants, citing literature on their role in transcriptional activity.

claim: H3K9ac1K14ac0 and H3K9ac1K14ac1 marks have been suggested as marks of transcriptionally active chromatin.
source: Moreover, when correlated with a panel of global histone modification levels, we found that TERTp mutants exhibited increased levels of H3K9ac1K14ac0 and H3K9ac1K14ac1 marks (Figure 4b), which have been suggested as marks of transcriptionally active chromatin (Ruthenburg et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the characterization of these histone marks.

claim: The TERT CGI (chr5:1,289,275–1,295,970) was the top correlate when H3K9ac1K14ac0 levels were compared against a genome-wide panel of CGI ASM levels.
source: Likewise, when H3K9ac1K14ac0 levels were compared against a genome-wide panel of CGI ASM levels, the TERT CGI (chr5:1,289,275–1,295,970) was the top correlate (Figure 4c).
evidence: The manuscript reports that the TERT CGI was the top correlate with H3K9ac1K14ac0 levels.

claim: H3K9ac1K14ac0 levels were significantly increased in TERTp mutants compared to monoallelic TERTp wild-type cell lines.
source: H3K9ac1K14ac0 levels were significantly increased in TERTp mutants compared to monoallelic TERTp wild-type cell lines, linking this histone modification to TERTp mutation (Figure 4d).
evidence: The manuscript reports significant increases in H3K9ac1K14ac0 levels in TERTp mutants.

claim: Among the top 1000 TERTpmut-hypomethylated CGIs, there was significant (FDR < 0.0001) and robust 10-fold enrichment for polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-repressed regions.
source: Among the top 1000 TERTpmut-hypomethylated CGIs (Figure 4a), we found significant (FDR < 0.0001) and robust 10-fold enrichment for polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-repressed regions (Figure 4e) previously characterized in several cell lines (HepG2, GM12878, HeLa-S3, K562, and HUVEC).
evidence: The manuscript reports significant enrichment of PRC2-repressed regions among hypomethylated CGIs.

claim: CGIs overlapping with PRC2-repressed segments were broadly hypomethylated in TERTpmut cell lines and accounted for nearly all the previously observed skew toward hypomethylation.
source: Beyond these top 1000 hypomethylated CGIs, CGIs overlapping with PRC2-repressed segments were broadly hypomethylated in TERTpmut cell lines and accounted for nearly all the previously observed skew toward hypomethylation (Figure 4f).
evidence: The manuscript reports that PRC2-repressed CGIs account for the hypomethylation skew in TERTpmut cell lines.

claim: The enrichment of PRC2 segments was much smaller (around 3.5-fold) in the H1-hESC cell line.
source: Interestingly, the enrichment of PRC2 segments was much smaller (around 3.5-fold) in the remaining profiled cell line, H1-hESC.
evidence: The manuscript reports a smaller enrichment of PRC2 segments in the H1-hESC cell line.

claim: Significant overlap was found with the H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 heterochromatin marks against ENCODE ChIP-seq peak region sets.
source: Against ENCODE ChIP-seq peak region sets, we also found significant overlap with the H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 heterochromatin marks (Figure 4g).
evidence: The manuscript reports significant overlap with specific heterochromatin marks.

claim: A moderate twofold (P = 5.1×10−24, Fisher's exact test) enrichment was observed for regions within 10 megabases of most telomeres.
source: Furthermore, we also observed a moderate twofold (P = 5.1×10−24, Fisher's exact test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a) enrichment for regions within 10 megabases of most telomeres, consistent with previous reports that PRC2-repressed and H3K27me3-marked regions are enriched in telomeric and subtelomeric regions (Rosenfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment for telomere-proximal regions, citing literature.

claim: PRC2-repressed and H3K27me3-marked regions are enriched in telomeric and subtelomeric regions.
source: Furthermore, we also observed a moderate twofold (P = 5.1×10−24, Fisher's exact test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a) enrichment for regions within 10 megabases of most telomeres, consistent with previous reports that PRC2-repressed and H3K27me3-marked regions are enriched in telomeric and subtelomeric regions (Rosenfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the enrichment of PRC2-repressed and H3K27me3-marked regions in telomeric and subtelomeric regions.

claim: The enrichment of hypomethylated regions among telomere-proximal regions may be indicative of a telomere position effect, which has been shown to affect the chromatin accessibility of the TERT locus.
source: The enrichment of these hypomethylated regions among telomere-proximal regions may also be indicative of a recently-reported telomere position effect, which has been shown to affect the chromatin accessibility of the TERT locus (Kim et al., 2016) located close to the chromosome 5 p telomere.
evidence: The manuscript speculates that the enrichment may be indicative of a telomere position effect, citing literature.

claim: PRC2 has previously been shown to exhibit allele-specific binding to the methylated silent allele in TERTpmut cell lines.
source: Given that PRC2 has previously been shown to exhibit allele-specific binding to the methylated silent allele in TERTpmut cell lines (Stern et al., 2017), this genome-wide pattern of hypomethylation at PRC2 sites suggests that background epigenetic events may interact with promoter mutations in facilitating TERT expression.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim about PRC2 allele-specific binding.

claim: The genome-wide pattern of hypomethylation at PRC2 sites suggests that background epigenetic events may interact with promoter mutations in facilitating TERT expression.
source: Given that PRC2 has previously been shown to exhibit allele-specific binding to the methylated silent allele in TERTpmut cell lines (Stern et al., 2017), this genome-wide pattern of hypomethylation at PRC2 sites suggests that background epigenetic events may interact with promoter mutations in facilitating TERT expression.
evidence: The manuscript speculates that background epigenetic events may interact with promoter mutations based on the observed hypomethylation pattern.

claim: CGI methylation levels were estimated across 878 TERT-expressing TCGA samples characterized with both the Illumina 450 k array and with a previously determined TERT promoter status.
source: To test this hypothesis, we estimated CGI methylation levels across 878 TERT-expressing TCGA samples characterized with both the Illumina 450 k array and with a previously determined TERT promoter status (Barthel et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of TCGA samples used for CGI methylation analysis.

claim: TERTpmut TCGA samples tended to exhibit hypomethylation at the cg11625005 methylation probe, consistent with previous analyses.
source: Consistent with previous analyses of TERT methylation levels at the cg11625005 methylation probe, we find that TERTpmut samples tended to exhibit hypomethylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports hypomethylation at a specific probe in TERTpmut TCGA samples, consistent with previous analyses.

claim: Among 13,547 CGIs in TCGA samples, an enrichment of hypomethylation of PRC2-overlapping CGIs was found.
source: Among 13,547 CGIs, we again found an enrichment of hypomethylation of PRC2-overlapping CGIs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), although this was less prominent than previously noted in the CCLE.
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment of hypomethylation of PRC2-overlapping CGIs in TCGA samples.

claim: LOLA enrichment analysis for TERTpmut-hypomethylated CGIs in the TCGA confirmed significant enrichments (FDR < 0.0001) of PRC2-repressed regions and associated histone modifications as the top enriched region sets.
source: LOLA enrichment analysis for TERTpmut-hypomethylated CGIs in the TCGA likewise confirmed significant enrichments (FDR < 0.0001) of PRC2-repressed regions and associated histone modifications as the top enriched region sets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: The manuscript reports significant enrichments of PRC2-repressed regions in TCGA samples.

claim: The fold-enrichment of PRC2-repressed regions in TCGA samples was less (about five-fold) than that observed in the CCLE samples.
source: However, the fold-enrichment was less (about five-fold) than that observed in the CCLE and did not display any significant enrichment in telomere-proximal regions (p = 0.70, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The manuscript reports a lower fold-enrichment in TCGA samples compared to CCLE samples.

claim: The skew toward hypomethylation in TERT promoter mutants among TCGA samples was weaker than in the CCLE samples, which may be the result of the more heterogeneous nature of primary TCGA samples as well as the differences in coverage between the Illumina 450 k array and RRBS.
source: Although the skew toward hypomethylation in TERT promoter mutants among these TCGA samples was weaker than in the CCLE samples, this may be the result of the more heterogeneous nature of primary TCGA samples as well as the differences in coverage between the Illumina 450 k array and RRBS.
evidence: The manuscript speculates that the weaker skew in TCGA samples may be due to sample heterogeneity and technical differences.

claim: Telomeres are repetitive nucleoprotein complexes located at chromosomal ends and are an important component of genomic stability.
source: Telomeres, repetitive nucleoprotein complexes located at chromosomal ends, are an important component of genomic stability (de Lange, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the characterization of telomeres.

claim: Telomeres prevent potentially lethal end-fusion events.
source: As protective chromosomal caps, telomeres prevent potentially lethal end-fusion events (McClintock, 1941; McClintock, 1942) and mis-processing of chromosomal ends as damaged sites by the DNA repair machinery (de Lange, 2005; Verdun and Karlseder, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the role of telomeres in preventing end-fusion events.

claim: Telomeres prevent mis-processing of chromosomal ends as damaged sites by the DNA repair machinery.
source: As protective chromosomal caps, telomeres prevent potentially lethal end-fusion events (McClintock, 1941; McClintock, 1942) and mis-processing of chromosomal ends as damaged sites by the DNA repair machinery (de Lange, 2005; Verdun and Karlseder, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the role of telomeres in preventing mis-processing by DNA repair machinery.

claim: Telomeres gradually shorten with successive rounds of cell division due to factors such as incomplete DNA replication and oxidative stress.
source: Due to factors such as incomplete DNA replication and oxidative stress, telomeres gradually shorten with successive rounds of cell division (Olovnikov, 1973).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that telomeres shorten with cell division.

claim: Telomere attrition eventually triggers growth arrest and senescence.
source: If left unchecked, telomere attrition eventually triggers growth arrest and senescence, and further shortening can lead to acute chromosomal breakage and cell death.
evidence: The manuscript states that telomere attrition triggers growth arrest and senescence.

claim: Further telomere shortening can lead to acute chromosomal breakage and cell death.
source: If left unchecked, telomere attrition eventually triggers growth arrest and senescence, and further shortening can lead to acute chromosomal breakage and cell death.
evidence: The manuscript states that further telomere shortening can lead to chromosomal breakage and cell death.

claim: Unrestricted telomere shortening acts as a major obstacle in the course of tumor development.
source: Unrestricted telomere shortening therefore acts as a major obstacle in the course of tumor development (Hackett and Greider, 2002; Lorbeer and Hockemeyer, 2020), and inhibition of telomere maintenance offers still largely untapped opportunities for targeted cancer therapies (Damm et al., 2001; Dikmen et al., 2005; Flynn et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that telomere shortening is an obstacle in tumor development.

claim: Inhibition of telomere maintenance offers still largely untapped opportunities for targeted cancer therapies.
source: Unrestricted telomere shortening therefore acts as a major obstacle in the course of tumor development (Hackett and Greider, 2002; Lorbeer and Hockemeyer, 2020), and inhibition of telomere maintenance offers still largely untapped opportunities for targeted cancer therapies (Damm et al., 2001; Dikmen et al., 2005; Flynn et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the potential of targeting telomere maintenance in cancer therapy.

claim: Telomere shortening in embryonic development and in certain adult cell populations is offset by telomerase.
source: Telomere shortening in embryonic development and in certain adult cell populations is offset by telomerase (Greider and Blackburn, 1985), a ribonucleoprotein enzyme with a core reverse transcriptase, TERT, that lengthens telomeres by catalyzing the addition of TTAGGG nucleotide repeats from an inbuilt RNA template component, TERC (Feng et al., 1995; Yu et al., 1990).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the role of telomerase in offsetting telomere shortening.

claim: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein enzyme with a core reverse transcriptase, TERT, that lengthens telomeres by catalyzing the addition of TTAGGG nucleotide repeats from an inbuilt RNA template component, TERC.
source: Telomere shortening in embryonic development and in certain adult cell populations is offset by telomerase (Greider and Blackburn, 1985), a ribonucleoprotein enzyme with a core reverse transcriptase, TERT, that lengthens telomeres by catalyzing the addition of TTAGGG nucleotide repeats from an inbuilt RNA template component, TERC (Feng et al., 1995; Yu et al., 1990).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the characterization of telomerase.

claim: Telomerase is transcriptionally silenced in the majority of somatic cells.
source: Although telomerase is transcriptionally silenced in the majority of somatic cells, telomerase is reactivated in over 85% of all human cancers (Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that telomerase is silenced in most somatic cells.

claim: Telomerase is reactivated in over 85% of all human cancers.
source: Although telomerase is transcriptionally silenced in the majority of somatic cells, telomerase is reactivated in over 85% of all human cancers (Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that telomerase is reactivated in most cancers.

claim: Most cancers tend to have shorter telomeres than normal tissues, perhaps due to telomere maintenance mechanisms developing only after a critical state of telomere crisis has been reached.
source: Despite having activated telomere maintenance mechanisms, most cancers tend to have shorter telomeres than normal tissues, perhaps due to telomere maintenance mechanisms developing only after a critical state of telomere crisis has been reached (Okamoto and Seimiya, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that cancers have shorter telomeres than normal tissues and speculates on the reason.

claim: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with highly recurrent mutations in the TERT promoter.
source: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with a diverse set of genomic alterations, the most common of which include highly recurrent mutations in the TERT promoter (Horn et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013), aberrant methylation (Lee et al., 2019) or copy number amplification (Zhang et al., 2000) of TERT, and modulation of the numerous transcription factors that regulate TERT expression (Greider, 2012; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the association between telomerase reactivation and TERT promoter mutations.

claim: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with aberrant methylation of TERT.
source: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with a diverse set of genomic alterations, the most common of which include highly recurrent mutations in the TERT promoter (Horn et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013), aberrant methylation (Lee et al., 2019) or copy number amplification (Zhang et al., 2000) of TERT, and modulation of the numerous transcription factors that regulate TERT expression (Greider, 2012; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the association between telomerase reactivation and aberrant TERT methylation.

claim: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with copy number amplification of TERT.
source: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with a diverse set of genomic alterations, the most common of which include highly recurrent mutations in the TERT promoter (Horn et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013), aberrant methylation (Lee et al., 2019) or copy number amplification (Zhang et al., 2000) of TERT, and modulation of the numerous transcription factors that regulate TERT expression (Greider, 2012; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the association between telomerase reactivation and TERT copy number amplification.

claim: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with modulation of the numerous transcription factors that regulate TERT expression.
source: Reactivation of telomerase is associated with a diverse set of genomic alterations, the most common of which include highly recurrent mutations in the TERT promoter (Horn et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2013), aberrant methylation (Lee et al., 2019) or copy number amplification (Zhang et al., 2000) of TERT, and modulation of the numerous transcription factors that regulate TERT expression (Greider, 2012; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the association between telomerase reactivation and transcription factor modulation.

claim: Many cancers that do not reactivate telomerase depend upon alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT).
source: Of the minority of cancers that do not reactivate telomerase, many depend upon alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), a process that exploits mechanisms of homologous recombination and is characterized by heterogeneous telomere lengths, mutations in the ATRX and DAXX chromatin-regulating factors, and genome instability (Cesare and Reddel, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the claim that cancers without telomerase reactivation often use ALT.

claim: ALT is a process that exploits mechanisms of homologous recombination and is characterized by heterogeneous telomere lengths, mutations in the ATRX and DAXX chromatin-regulating factors, and genome instability.
source: Of the minority of cancers that do not reactivate telomerase, many depend upon alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), a process that exploits mechanisms of homologous recombination and is characterized by heterogeneous telomere lengths, mutations in the ATRX and DAXX chromatin-regulating factors, and genome instability (Cesare and Reddel, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to support the characterization of ALT.
